title: Supply-Chain Security, Headers & Logging
objectives: Assess dependency risk: typosquatting, malicious scripts, abandoned packages
Use lockfiles, pinning and automated audits as supply-chain controls
Ship the standard security header set and know what each one buys
Log security events usefully — and know what must never be logged
body:
Modern apps are mostly other people's code, served with your headers, and observed by your logs. Supply-chain hygiene decides whether a compromised dependency reaches production; security headers decide how much a browser can be tricked into doing on your pages; logging discipline decides whether an incident is Investigable in minutes or writes credentials into log storage.

## The problem
A fresh contributor adds a package that looks like your favorite linter but is a typosquat with a postinstall exfiltration script; meanwhile production serves no HSTS and the auth middleware logs full request bodies — including passwords — to a third-party log service. Three different controls, one shared root cause: nobody owned the pipeline around the code.

## Constraints
- npm install runs lifecycle scripts by default; a typosquatted name one letter off is enough to execute code on every developer machine.
- A committed lockfile pins exact versions; without it, two installs of the same package.json can produce different trees.
- Audit tools only know about *reported* CVEs — they are necessary, not sufficient.
- Headers are per-response and mostly free; their value is making common browser attacks structurally harder.
- Logs are frequently forwarded, shared and retained far beyond the app's lifetime — treat every log line as public until proven otherwise.

## Options
```json
{
  "supplyChain": {
    "lockfile": "commit package-lock.json; review lock diffs in PRs",
    "versions": "exact or tilde pins; updates via renovate/dependabot PRs, never blanket latest",
    "audit": "npm audit / osv-scanner in CI, fail on high severity",
    "hygiene": "fewer dependencies, verify names letter-by-letter, prefer scoped/well-known packages"
  },
  "headers": {
    "Strict-Transport-Security": "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains — forces HTTPS after first visit",
    "X-Content-Type-Options": "nosniff — browser must honor declared content type",
    "Content-Security-Policy": "default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none' — limits script and framing",
    "Referrer-Policy": "strict-origin-when-cross-origin — trim what leaves via Referer",
    "Permissions-Policy": "camera=(), geolocation=() — deny browser features you do not use"
  },
  "logging": {
    "log": "login success/failure, permission denials, validation rejects, admin actions",
    "never": "passwords, tokens, cookies, full card numbers, government ids"
  }
}
```

## Tradeoffs
Strict pinning keeps versions frozen until someone drives updates; automated dependency PRs restore currency at the cost of review bandwidth. Aggressive headers (tight CSP, long HSTS) can break embedded widgets or subdomains that are not yet HTTPS — roll out with report-only mode first. Logging auth failures in detail aids detection and creates a data-protection surface if details include credentials or personal data.

## Decision
Commit the lockfile, pin versions, run audits in CI, and add dependencies reluctantly. Ship the full header set: HSTS, nosniff, CSP (start report-only), Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy. Log security events with actor, action, outcome and correlation id — never secrets, tokens, credentials or government identifiers; redact request bodies by default.

## Measure it
Scan responses with a header checker (securityheaders-style) before and after; fail CI on missing headers via an integration test. Track dependency counts and audit findings over time; budget review time for update PRs. For logging, sample production log storage and grep it for token and password field names — a hit means redaction is broken, and that check belongs in CI against fixtures.

## Best practices
- Commit the lockfile; review dependency diffs, not just code diffs.
- Run dependency audit and secret scanning in CI on every push.
- Ship HSTS, nosniff, CSP, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy on all responses.
- Log security-relevant events: auth outcomes, authorization denials, validation rejects, admin actions.
- Redact by default: bodies, cookies and authorization headers never reach log storage raw.

## Common mistakes
- Typing a package name from memory in a hurry — typosquatting targets exactly that.
- Deleting the lockfile to 'fix' a conflict, silently floating every transitive dependency.
- Enabling HSTS with includeSubDomains before every subdomain serves valid HTTPS.
- Logging Authorization headers or request bodies 'temporarily' during debugging — and forgetting forever.
- Treating a green npm audit as security proof while ignoring abandoned, unreported packages.

## Production considerations
- Alert on new dependencies in PRs without a lockfile diff review; supply-chain review is part of code review, not an afterthought.
- Generate an SBOM in builds so you can answer 'do we run X?' within minutes of the next ecosystem disclosure.
- Set HSTS in stages (short max-age, then long, then preload consideration) and own every subdomain's HTTPS first.
- Keep log retention and access control deliberate: security logs are sensitive data and need their own access rules.

examples.name: headers-and-logs.json

exercise.prompt: Audit a production response's security headers and its log events. Render a verdict per expected header: present or missing with the one-line consequence. Then classify each log event as safe-to-log or never-log: login failure with ip (safe), request with Authorization header value (never), admin delete with actor id (safe), raw request body with password field (never). Implement both auditors.
hints: Header audit: check the present map first, then describe what the missing header would have defended against.
CSP, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy are missing in the fixture — say what each buys.
Event audit is a lookup: safe kinds pass, never kinds name the leaked credential class.

questions.prompt: Why is a committed lockfile a security control?
options: It pins exact dependency versions so builds are reproducible and reviewed diffs actually mean something
It blocks lifecycle scripts from running
questions.explanation: Without a lockfile, identical installs can pull different transitive versions; the lockfile makes the dependency tree deterministic and reviewable.

questions.prompt: Which set of items must never appear in security logs?
options: User ids, action names, correlation ids
Passwords, session tokens, cookies, full card numbers
questions.explanation: Credential material in logs turns your logging pipeline into a breach surface; diagnostic fields like ids, IPs and reasons are exactly what should be logged instead.
